# G1 perceptive WMAC: principles, gradients, and reproduction from scratch

Source snapshot: November 20, 2026. Hiking training v3 uses checkpoint architecture 9. This guide targets a separate Linux machine with access to the public GitHub projects and this document. It needs neither access to the original workstation nor its shared drive.

Chapters 4–8 derive the networks, GenCoord, visual latents, AMP, and BPTT. Chapter 9 explains integration changes. Chapter 10 describes the 26 rewards. Chapter 11 specifies the physics assets, task, camera, and data. Chapters 12–15 cover execution, training, evaluation, troubleshooting, and verification. Appendix A contains the complete scripts. Appendix B supplies the source and data required to reproduce the project from this single file.

## 1. Reproduction goals and how to use this guide

### 1.1 Pinned configuration

The training entry point is `scripts/train_wmac_perceptive.py`. A new run uses the following defaults.

| Component | Pinned protocol |
| --- | --- |
| Task | `Unitree-G1-AMP-Perceptive-Hiking` |
| Learning framework | SuperMimic-style simulator collection, world-model fitting, and imagined actor–critic updates with backpropagation through time (BPTT) |
| Physics representation | `supermimic_gencoord_v1`, 0.02 s per control step, 4 physics substeps |
| Vision | `instinct_latent_v1`, 8 depth images jointly encoded into a 128-dimensional latent |
| Camera | `g1_hiking_calibrated_v1`, fixed Hiking mounting pose and measured G1 intrinsics. Pixel and mounting randomization are off by default. |
| Environment objective | `hiking_full_v1`, the 26 Hiking rewards for the standard unshod G1 |
| Data | `hiking_walk_v1` + `pre_hiking_local_walk_turn_v2`. The full official walking sequence, 13 historical walking/turning clips, and their mirrors. No standing supplement by default. |
| AMP | `hiking_v1`, 67 features per frame and 10 frames of history. Discriminator training and actor input gradients are handled separately. |
| Training revision | `hiking_training_version=3` and checkpoint `architecture_version=9` |
| Robot | Official unshod `G1ParkourRoughEnvCfg` torso-base URDF physics adapted to the local pelvis-root GenCoord representation |
| Actor | Dense four-expert mixture of experts (MoE) by default. Use `--actor-type transformer` for the attention actor. |
| Execution | `execution_profile=supermimic`, `training_schedule=supermimic_v1`, Muon + Adam, TF32, compilation, GPU replay, and CUDA Graphs |

Training covers forward walking, left and right turns, in-place turns, and traversal of complex terrain. Getting up, running, sidestepping, and backward motion fall outside the task. The repository retains PPO-AMP, the flat-ground `train_wmac.py`, the legacy pixel world model, and the earlier RPL full-image protocol for backward compatibility. The defaults documented here apply to the new entry point.

Reproduction has two levels. The first rebuilds the same source, assets, protocols, dependencies, and closed training loop. The second measures policy capability after retraining. This guide covers the first level in full and provides training and evaluation commands for the second. No previous model weights are supplied. Retraining can produce different checkpoint bytes. Passing a short integration test gives no measure of standing, walking, or terrain traversal.

### 1.2 Why cloning the original repository is insufficient

The original public project is [ccrpRepo/AMP_mjlab](https://github.com/ccrpRepo/AMP_mjlab). The appendix pins its public base to `6c7a2947fccc973e4af8e6d90e550400f1b6fcfc`. The source workstation's Git HEAD was `6427e3eed1ea48d0167c594d964550e05fae38a1`. Uncommitted changes and new perceptive code, including the v3 configuration, also contributed to this framework. That workstation's `origin` points to a private CodeHub instance.

The appendix encodes the required source changes, licenses, camera parameters, official motion sources, new URDF and head assets, and compatibility data. The restoration script obtains the pinned public GitHub commit, restores these files, and verifies their SHA-256 hashes. **The public GitHub base and this complete document together supply the reproduction inputs.** Keep the appendix data with the main text.

The Hiking authors released the official walking NPZ in their public data package, separately from the original AMP GitHub repository. The older G1 standing CSV is historical compatibility data outside the official Hiking release. The default 13 historical walking/turning clips are selected anew from public base assets and mirrored. A new machine can build them without the source workstation, its cache or shared drive, Google Drive, a private CodeHub instance, or additional download locations.

### 1.3 Feishu formatting and file preservation

The main text uses standard Markdown headings, tables, and code blocks. Every key equation has a plain-text version that works independently of LaTeX, Mermaid, HTML, external images, or local paths. You can copy the main text into a Feishu cloud document.

The long appendix blocks are also plain text. Keep the complete original UTF-8 `.md` file to restore the program on another machine. Screenshots and ellipses copied from collapsed blocks omit data. The script checks block numbering/order, missing blocks, and SHA-256 integrity. It stops when validation fails. An export may change formatting if the data blocks and markers survive intact. Successful final verification determines whether the export is usable.


### 1.4 Changes since the November 17 guide

The November 20, 2026 working tree is the source of record. Check the source directly when the older README text or `SOURCE_SNAPSHOT` date is stale.

| Component | Previous guide (v2) | Current default (v3) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Physics assets | Historical G1 MJCF physics | Official unshod torso-base URDF physics with pelvis-root state storage |
| Material conditioning / context | 33 collision geoms / 133 dimensions | 29 collision geoms / 129 dimensions |
| World-model input / RunningNorm | 439 input dimensions, joint statistics over 311 | 435 input dimensions, RunningNorm on the 97 state and processed-action dimensions only |
| Critic input / value cap | 315 dimensions / 61.4 | 281 dimensions / 40.8 (current clipping heuristic) |
| Depth camera | `g1_hiking_dr_v1`, RPL-style randomization on | `g1_hiking_calibrated_v1`, fixed calibrated camera, randomization off |
| Action | Raw action clipped to ±20 | `action_limit=None`. Physical actuator effort limits remain active. |
| Expert data | Full Hiking data and locked-pose standing, 4 clips | Full Hiking data plus 13 historical walking/turning clips and mirrors, 28 clips |
| Sampling clock | `iterations` counts learner macro-updates | `iterations` counts vector control steps across parallel environments |
| Budget / saving | 320,000 macro-updates / every 2,000 updates | 1,000,000 control steps / every 1,000 learner updates |
| Validation split | 10% of environments held out | 0 by default, no dedicated holdout environments |
| Actor | MoE | MoE by default, with an explicit Transformer comparison option |

These changes affect network inputs, checkpoint metadata, and both the physics and data distributions. Resuming an old checkpoint keeps its saved protocol. “Current” in this guide means v3. Older protocol parameters appear for comparison and compatibility. Although v3 has no separate standing expert, it includes zero-speed commands, stopping at navigation targets, and the `stand_still` reward.

### 1.5 Training version 4: realignment with the original Hiking task (November 26, 2026)

Fresh runs now use `hiking_training_version=4`. It keeps the SuperMimic world model, imagined actor–critic and execution profile of version 3 unchanged, and returns the task to InstinctLab `de6b92f` wherever MuJoCo allows. Network inputs and checkpoint architecture (version 9) are the same as version 3. `--hiking-training-version 3` reproduces the previous protocol, and version 3 checkpoints resume, play and evaluate with the protocol they saved. **Where a later chapter describes the camera intrinsics, the expert pool or the edge geometry, it describes version 3; this section states the version 4 behaviour.**

| Component | Version 3 | Version 4 (default) | Hiking source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Camera rays | `g1_hiking_calibrated_v1`: measured G1 RealSense intrinsics, 88.92° × 58.11°, off-centre principal point | `hiking_depth_only_v1`: Hiking's pinhole, 89.51° × 58.29°, centred, pixel centres at index + 0.5. Rays match IsaacLab's pattern to 3e-6°. | `parkour_env_cfg.py:359-365` |
| AMP reference | Official sequence plus 13 local clips, uniform random ten-frame windows | Official sequence only. One timeline per robot: start uniform in [0, 0.9) of the clip, mirrored with probability 0.5, first frame fills the history on reset. | `g1_parkour_target_amp_cfg.py:33-44` |
| Discriminator logit-layer L2 | 0.04 | 1.0 | See below |
| Terrain edges for `volume_points_penetration` | Detected on the MuJoCo heightfield triangles and on each box separately | Detected on Hiking's terrain mesh: IsaacLab's height-field mesh with `slope_threshold=1`, walls, rotated boxes and the flat mesh-box ground, merged as `TerrainImporter.import_mesh` does | `terrain_importer.py:53-68`, `edge_cylinder.py:45-75` |
| First reset | Robots keep the sampled terrain level (0–5) | Every robot starts one level lower (floor 0), as IsaacLab's first `env.reset()` runs the curriculum with zero scores | `curriculums.py:47-51` |
| Robot variant | Unshod only | Unshod by default; `--robot-variant shoe` selects the registered task's shod robot | `g1_parkour_target_amp_cfg.py:96-101` |

**Edges.** In the source mesh every rise steeper than 45° between neighbouring height samples becomes a vertical face, so the lip and the crease of each step are 90° edges. On the MuJoCo heightfield the same step is a ramp across one 0.05 m cell with dihedral atan(h/0.05), which passes the 70° test only for h above about 0.137 m. Version 3 therefore had almost no edge cylinders on stairs in the easier half of the difficulty range and on low boxes. Version 4 rebuilds the source mesh from the same integer height arrays (`hiking_geometry.py:hiking_source_terrain_mesh`) and applies the unchanged 70°/30°/0.05 m greedy concatenation. Checked against InstinctLab's and IsaacLab's own functions executed on one 12-tile terrain: identical sharp-edge set (20,643 edges), cylinder count (3,839) and total length. Collision, depth images and the foot height rays still use the MuJoCo heightfield, where the riser is the one-cell ramp. The ramp occupies the 0.05 m in front of the source riser, which is the same strip the source crease cylinder (radius 0.05 m) penalises.

**Logit-layer L2.** Hiking's agent config sets `discriminator_logit_weight_decay_coef = 0.04`. `instinct_rl` `574c8d5` stores the term under the loss key `logit_weight_decay` and looks its coefficient up as `logit_weight_decay_coef`, an attribute that does not exist, so the default 1.0 applies (`wasabi.py:152,208-215`); 0.04 only switches the term on. Version 4 uses the executed value. `--discriminator-head-weight-decay 0.04` selects the configured one.

**Robot variants.** Hiking has two G1 configurations. `G1ParkourRoughEnvCfg` is unshod with reset-sampled actuator delay of 0–2 physics steps. `G1ParkourEnvCfg`, the one registered as `Instinct-Parkour-Target-Amp-G1-v0`, applies `ShoeConfigMixin`: the seven collision capsules under each foot move from z = -0.025 m to -0.048 m, the foot volume points from z ∈ [-0.04, 0] to [-0.063, -0.023], and the `feet_at_plane` offset from 0.035 m to 0.058 m. Because the mixin replaces the robot after the delayed actuators were assigned, that task runs the undelayed actuator set. `--robot-variant shoe` reproduces all four changes. The default stays unshod because the deployment interface and the Unitree-model sim-to-sim of this project describe a bare-foot G1.

**Remaining differences from Hiking, all outside the learner.**

- Collision and depth geometry: by default a MuJoCo heightfield with one-cell ramps where the source mesh has vertical risers (up to the step height inside one 0.05 m cell). The real-robot options below remove this for depth and halve it for collision.
- Contact solver, friction combination for robot–robot contacts (MuJoCo takes the larger coefficient, PhysX multiplies), restitution and the PhysX joint-velocity limit have no MuJoCo counterpart.
- Terrain random streams: the source seeds tile content from the run seed and tile difficulty from a fixed seed; here one generator seeded by the run seed draws both. The distributions are the same.
- Camera refresh late in an episode: IsaacLab compares float32 sensor timestamps against the 0.02 s update period. Replaying that arithmetic (not a run of IsaacLab) gives a fresh frame every second control step during the last 4 s of a 20 s episode. Here the camera refreshes every control step throughout.

**Training version 5: real-robot defaults (November 27, 2026).** Fresh runs now use `hiking_training_version=5`, which is version 4 with three defaults changed: `depth_geometry="source_mesh"`, `collision_horizontal_scale=0.025` and `robot_dynamics_randomization="unitree_g1_v1"` (the README's sim-to-sim section describes the randomization; it appends four columns to the 129-column world-model and critic context). Each stays a separate flag, `--hiking-training-version 4` selects the Hiking-aligned task without them, and version 4 runs and checkpoints are unchanged. The first two options also apply to version 3. Checkpoints written before an option existed load `depth_geometry="collision"` and `robot_dynamics_randomization="none"`.

| Option | Effect | Implementation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--depth-geometry source_mesh` | The depth camera's terrain rays hit Hiking's vertical-riser mesh instead of the collision heightfield. | Each tile's IsaacLab mesh is added as a mesh geom with `contype=conaffinity=0` in geom group 0 (a flat box for level ground). The heightfields move to group 4, outside the camera's groups (0, 2). `terrain.py:_hiking_full_terrain` |
| `--collision-horizontal-scale 0.025` | Collision heightfield on a 2.5 cm grid, so each riser's ramp is one 2.5 cm cell. | The grid samples the upper surface of the same mesh (`hiking_geometry.py:source_mesh_height_grid`); a sample on a riser takes its top, so plateaus keep their source extent. The 161 × 161 source integers are stored beside each heightfield as a MuJoCo numeric, and edge detection reads them, so the edge cylinders are identical. `njmax` rises from 700 to 1024 because host MuJoCo makes one contact per prism under each foot at initialization. |
| `evaluate_wmac_perceptive.py --terrain-geometry real_robot` | Evaluates any Hiking checkpoint with both options. | Overrides the two fields of the loaded configuration. |

Checks, on an RTX 4080:

- Refined grid against brute-force rays on the mesh: equal within 1 mm on four terrain families. It never lies below the mesh (minimum -0.9 mm), and it departs from the mesh by more than 1 cm over 1.5% of the mesh area, against 2.9% for the 0.05 m heightfield.
- In-environment depth: terrain rays against host `mj_ray` on the same geometry agree within 6 µm with and without the options. With `source_mesh` no camera ray ends on a heightfield.
- What the camera sees against what the feet touch, along camera rays in training: up to 7.2 cm apart with the mesh over the 0.05 m heightfield, up to 3.6 cm over the 0.025 m one.
- Cost with both options: simulator step +13% at 1024 robots; compiled training iteration 0.2414 s against 0.2316 s at 256 robots (+4%); about 1.1 GB more GPU memory; one-time kernel compilation of about 150 s.
- `sensor_transform.pt` (version 3) on the new geometry: 10.4% of episodes fall against 10.2% on its training geometry, 2.33 m of target progress per start on both (512 robots, 500 steps).
- On the 0.025 m grid MuJoCo-Warp reports `height field collision overflow` when one geom penetrates 50 or more prisms: 60 times in 256,000 robot-steps with that policy, 123 times in 184,000 robot-steps at the start of training. The foot capsules are 2 cm wide and stay below the limit; the reports come from fallen robots, which terminate.

**Resources at the reference scale, version 5 defaults (measured November 27, 2026 on an RTX 4080 with 16 GB and extrapolated).**

| Resource | Estimate for 4,096 robots | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GPU memory | 60–70 GB peak, so an 80 GB card | Simulator about 28 GB (6.4 MB per robot plus 2.5 GB, measured at 256–1,536 robots). Learner about 24 GB at the default actor batch of 4,096 (7.9, 9.3 and 14.2 GB measured at 512, 1,024 and 2,048). Replay and other per-robot tensors 10–17 GB. |
| Time for 1,000,000 vector steps | About 8 days at RTX 4080 speed | 400,000 learner updates at about 0.9 s (world model 0.39 s measured; actor–critic 0.17 s and 0.28 s measured at batches of 1,024 and 2,048), plus 1,000,000 simulator steps at about 0.36 s (0.069–0.165 s measured at 256–1,536 robots). |
| Host memory | 12 GB used by the process; 32 GB recommended | Measured; it does not grow with the robot count. |
| CPU | One fast core is the limit; the process uses about 1.5 cores | Measured. About 0.05 s of every simulator step is fixed Python overhead. |
| Disk | About 45 GB per run | A checkpoint of 111 MB every 1,000 learner updates. |

None of these was run at 4,096 robots: the card used for the measurements has 16 GB, and the default learner alone exceeds it. Each figure is a straight-line extrapolation from the sizes listed.

Version 5 costs about 1.7 GB more GPU memory than version 4 at this scale (simulator 28.5 GB against 26.8 GB) and about 11% more simulator time per step. The update-to-data ratio follows the robot count (`utd = 0.4` at 4,096), which is why 1,000,000 vector steps make 400,000 learner updates.

**Simulator and learner on separate GPUs (November 27, 2026).** `--sim-device cuda:1` builds the environment on a second card while networks, replay and imagination stay on `--device`. The environment keeps its own state adapter; the runner imagines with `learner_adapter(env.adapter, device)`, a copy whose tensors (kinematic tree, reward constants, terrain heights, edge cylinders, box tables) live on the learner's card and whose `state()`, `command()` and `context()` still read the simulator. Collection crosses the boundary in three places per control step (`_from_env` for the observation, the transition and the depth frame; `_to_env` for the action), about 176 MB at 4,096 robots. With one device these calls return their argument. `sim_device` is excluded from the saved protocol and reset on every checkpoint load. Checks: the copy against the environment's adapter on eleven functions used by imagination (identical on one device; within 2e-5 between CPU and CUDA); a run with the simulator on the CPU and the learner on CUDA with graph-captured world-model, actor and critic updates, checkpoint, resume (split and single device) and evaluation. Two CUDA devices together were not available for testing.

**Camera on the robot.** `unitree_interface.RealSenseDepthAdapter` converts the robot's raw depth image (480 × 270 Z16 at 60 Hz, `fx = fy = 244.496`, `cx = 244.612`, `cy = 132.597`, bundled as `src/assets/cameras/g1_depth_calibration_480x270_60hz.json`) into the training frame. Every training pixel reads the nearest RealSense pixel on its ray; depth along the optical axis is unchanged because the two cameras share an optical centre. Only training column 63 falls outside the real image, and the policy crops columns 0–15 and 48–63 away. Holes (no measurement, or depth below 0.2 m) are filled from measured neighbours inside rows 18–35, columns 16–47, following the rule of `instinct_onboard`'s `parkour_agent.py` with a NumPy neighbour average in place of `cv2.inpaint`. On a synthetic floor with a 0.17 m step the lookup is within 3.0 mm of the training camera (mean 1.1 mm); resizing the image as if it were the training pinhole, which is what `instinct_onboard` does, is off by 5.2 mm on average and 11.5 mm at most. The camera-to-torso mount has not been measured: the capture report holds only the factory depth-to-color transform. A measured orientation can be passed to the adapter, which then corrects it exactly (3° of pitch left uncorrected costs 36 mm on average in the same scene); a position offset needs retraining.

## 2. Architecture and public sources

### 2.1 One training cycle

```text
Real MuJoCo-Warp environment (outside backpropagation)
  Proprioceptive history [8 × 96] ────┐
  Depth history [8 × 18 × 32] → E → z128 ─┴→ Actor (4-expert MoE or attention) → 29 joint actions
  Real successors and contact/torque labels                                              │
           │                                                                             ↓
           └────────────────→ Replay ←──────────────────────────────────── next real control step
                               │
        ┌──────────────────────┼────────────────────────┐
        ↓                      ↓                        ↓
  Fit multistep WM       Train D on real AMP windows   Sample imagination starting states
  + encoder/decoder reconstruction                     │
                                                       ↓
                      Freeze WM, D, and critic parameters. Imagine H=32 steps.
                      (state,z) → action → WM → (next_state,next_z)
                                                       │
                      Hiking task reward + AMP style reward + terminal value
                                                       │
                                     Update actor by BPTT
                                                       ↓
                              Fix imagined targets and update critic separately
```

The world model learns a differentiable approximation of simulator transitions. Contact, camera rays, and resets in the physics simulator can remain ordinary simulation operations. The actor update differentiates through the learned world model. The physical environment supplies supervision and evaluation trajectories.

### 2.2 Contributions of the source projects

| Source | Components used here | Implementation details |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Original AMP_mjlab | Public visual meshes and historical motions, the local AMP codebase, mjlab and rsl_rl interfaces | Its PPO update does not differentiate state through the model and discriminator. |
| AMP | Matching expert and policy motion distributions using a discriminator-derived style reward | This implementation uses Hiking/WASABI's ten-frame representation and loss details, which differ from the original AMP experiments. |
| Official SuperMimic | GenCoord velocity increments, supervision of integrated state, real replay, short imagined BPTT, survival weighting, terminal critic, reference optimizer and execution scale | The official task tracks motions. Here the task, AMP, vision, and physical auxiliary labels follow Hiking, with v3 input and data protocols. |
| InstinctMJ `supermimic` | Joint depth-history latent, reconstruction-trained encoder, visual stop-gradient, residual latent prediction | This is the principal open-source implementation of images in the differentiable world model. The integration retains the local GenCoord and mjlab task interfaces. |
| Hiking / InstinctLab / instinct_rl | Unshod URDF physics, depth preprocessing, MoE, complete walking data, AMP representation, 26 rewards, 10 terrain types, commands, actuator delays, training and PLAY rules | The physical backend is MuJoCo-Warp. Pointwise equivalence with PhysX dynamics is unverified. |
| RPL / Holosoma | Relative depth noise, dropped points, terrain-biased edge occlusion, and mounting/FOV uncertainty | The RPL randomization code and legacy protocol are retained, with randomization disabled by default in v3. The PPO/DAgger pipeline and external front/rear camera layout were not imported. |

The method references are the [AMP paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.02180) and the [SuperMimic paper on world-model policy gradients](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28480). The bundled implementation defines the specific formulas, dimensions, and detach operations described below.

## 3. Restoring the framework from the public upstream project

### 3.1 System requirements

The full configuration targets Linux x86_64 and an NVIDIA CUDA GPU. Its reference scale is 4,096 parallel environments, horizon H32, a three-layer world model of width 2,048, and GPU replay with 1,000 vector time steps. The hardware target is an 80 GB GPU. A fixed replay memory estimate covers only part of peak process memory. Run the small integration test first on lower-memory machines. Reduced scale changes the experimental conditions.

Install a compatible NVIDIA driver, `git`, `curl`, `bzip2`, `tar`, and Python 3 to run the restorer. The installation script downloads a pinned Miniforge release and creates a separate Python 3.11.17 environment, independent of any existing Conda environment. Ubuntu 22.04 or 24.04 x86_64 is recommended. The pinned binary wheels require a recent glibc, so check compatibility on older distributions. For example, install the system tools with:

```bash
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y git curl ca-certificates bzip2 tar python3 libegl1 libgl1 libglib2.0-0
nvidia-smi
```

The system package manager need not provide Python 3.11. The host NVIDIA driver must support the CUDA 12.6 runtime bundled with the pinned PyTorch wheels. A separate CUDA compiler toolchain is generally unnecessary. Test CUDA directly to confirm GPU availability.

The source code and motion assets require no private resources. Python packages still come from PyPI and the PyTorch wheel index. If those endpoints are inaccessible, prepare a wheelhouse on a connected system of the same platform, then install the dependencies from it. The appendix installer lists the exact endpoints and versions.

### 3.2 Restoration and verification sequence

Appendix A contains the complete scripts. On the new machine:

1. Save this complete Markdown document.
2. Copy the appendix restorer into a Python file and run it to reconstruct the base directory from the pinned public GitHub commit and decode the bundled overlay.
3. Run the installation script in the restored directory. It creates a fresh Python environment, installs pinned dependencies, applies the mjlab observation-history patch, and checks the MuJoCo-Warp height-field source. Applying the height-field fix requires explicit opt-in.
4. Verify the official raw motion source, rebuild the 13 historical supplemental clips and the complete default 28-clip expert pool offline, then run the data audit and core CPU regressions.
5. Run the small GPU training test. Verify actual collection, world-model fitting, actor/critic updates, and AMP updates.
6. Start a separate full training experiment as described in Chapter 13, then evaluate it independently in the physics simulator.

The restorer checks file contents. CPU regressions test operators and protocols. The small GPU run tests the training loop. Full physical evaluation after training measures policy capability. Each result addresses a different question.

Default output directories are ordinary local directories. The restorer does not recreate the original workstation's shared-drive symlinks for `logs` or `.perceptive_cache`. It refuses to overwrite a nonempty destination. Use a separate destination when testing it on the source machine.

## 4. Current defaults, state, and network interfaces

The configuration from `parse_config([])` selects Hiking training v3 and the four-expert Hiking MoE actor. Start a separate experiment with `--actor-type transformer` to use attention. The two actors share the visual encoder, world model, rewards, AMP and training schedule. They have different policy functions and parameter counts, so a MoE checkpoint cannot resume directly as an attention actor.

### 4.1 Physical state and network dimensions

The GenCoord physical state has 71 dimensions.

```text
s = [p_world(3), quaternion_wxyz(4), v_world(3), omega_world(3),
     joint_position(29), joint_velocity(29)]

gencoord(s) = [root_world_Z(1), gravity_body(3), v_body(3), omega_body(3),
              joint_position(29), joint_velocity(29)]  # 68 dimensions
```

The v3 G1 uses the inertias, collision bodies, and joint geometry of the pinned Hiking URDF. Local pelvis-root storage represents motion from the source torso-root model. The 29 active collision geoms follow a fixed name order, with their applied sliding friction in `context[100:129]`, giving 129 context dimensions. The v2 asset had 33 geoms and a 133-dimensional context. Migration requires more than renaming the version or reusing the old shapes.

The complete world-model input is

```text
u_joint = raw_action * joint_position_scale + joint_position_offset  # 29
x_state_action = concat(gencoord(s), u_joint)                       # 97
x_WM = concat(
    RunningNorm(x_state_action),          # 97, statistics update continuously
    range_normalized_context,             # 129, no RunningNorm
    terrain_patch_9x9,                    # 81, no RunningNorm
    (z-z_mean)/z_std                       # 128
)                                         # 435 dimensions in total

F: 435 -> 2048 -> 2048 -> 2048 -> 176
176 = physical_velocity_delta35 + auxiliary13 + latent_delta128
```

Hidden layers use GELU and LayerNorm. In v3, only the first 97 inputs update empirical moments, with `max_count=inf`. Context uses `(mu-.95)/.65` for the mean friction and the 29 per-geom friction values. Subtracting 1 maps the 29 actuator substep lags from 0/1/2 to −1/0/1. Other context columns keep their original values. World Z is used without first subtracting terrain height. The action scale and offset come directly from the actual environment's joint-position action term buffers.

```python
# src/wmac_perceptive/latent_models.py:154–183
if self.reference_inputs:
    action = action * self.action_scale + self.action_offset
    context = normalize_hiking_sim_context(context)
else:
    ground = self.terrain_oracle.height_at(state[..., :2])
    state = torch.cat((state[..., :2],
        (state[..., 2]-ground).unsqueeze(-1), state[..., 3:]), -1)
raw = torch.cat((gencoord_features(state), action, context, patch), -1)
# v3 uses dim=97. The following context and patch bypass empirical normalization.
dim = self.in_norm.mean.numel()
physical = torch.cat((self.in_norm(raw[..., :dim]), raw[..., dim:]), -1)
```

The final layer's 35 physical-output rows keep the default `nn.Linear` initialization. The 13 auxiliary and 128 latent output rows have zero weights. Auxiliary outputs use a bias of −4 followed by softplus. The zero initialization of the 35 physics rows belonged to v2.

The critic takes 281 inputs.

```text
x_critic = concat(gencoord(s)[68], command[3],
                  normalize_hiking_sim_context(context)[129], terrain_patch[81])
# 68 + 3 + 129 + 81 = 281
```

The previous raw action is already in `context[38:67]`, so no extra 29 dimensions are concatenated. The critic retains hidden widths 256/128 with Linear → LayerNorm → GELU and does not use its input RunningNorm buffer. The actor reads 768 proprioceptive dimensions and the 128 visual latent dimensions. It has no access to the 129 context or the 81 terrain dimensions.

### 4.2 Default MoE actor

The visual encoder maps a joint 8×18×32 depth-only stack to z128 using `Conv2d(8,4,kernel3,padding1)→ReLU→MaxPool2d(2)→flatten576→Linear256/ReLU→Linear256/ReLU→Linear128`. Hiking preprocessing crops the raw 36×64 frames to 18×32. The diagnostic validity channel stays outside the CNN. The actor input has 896 dimensions. Its linear gate performs 896→4→Softmax, and all four experts contribute to the dense mixture. Each expert uses 896→256→128→64→29 with ELU. The actor uses neither input RunningNorm nor output tanh. V3 leaves the raw action unclamped. Physical collection adds exploration noise with std=.1. The joint-position transform, PD control, and physical effort saturation operate downstream of the policy's raw action.

## 5. SuperMimic GenCoord world model: derivation and supervision

The prediction `Delta=[dv_b(3),domega_b(3),dv_j(29)]` contains velocity increments over one complete control step. The outputs are expressed in velocity units. They represent neither accelerations nor pose residuals and are not normalized by an output standard deviation.

The control period is `dt=.02s`, with `D=4` physics substeps of `.005s`. Suppose the full-step change `dv` is distributed uniformly across D substeps. Semi-implicit Euler updates velocity before position at each substep, giving

`p_next=p + (dt/D)*sum_{i=1}^D(v+i*dv/D)=p+dt*(v+c*dv)`, where `c=(D+1)/(2D)=5/8`.

The local implementation uses the following updates.

`v'_w=R(q)*(v_b+dv_b)` and `omega'_w=R(q)*(omega_b+domega_b)`.

`p'=p+dt*R(q)*(v_b+c*dv_b)`.

`q'=normalize(ExpQuaternion(dt*R(q)*(omega_b+c*domega_b))*q)`.

`q'_j=q_j+dt*(v_j+c*dv_j)` and `v'_j=v_j+dv_j`.

The quaternion increment multiplies from the left because the twist is in the world frame. `ExpQuaternion` uses `sqrt(||omega*dt||²+1e-8)` for a finite derivative at zero angular velocity. The learned velocity increments already include gravity, contact, and PD effects, so the integrator adds no explicit gravity term. See `gencoord.py:64,106–143`.

Supervision applies after integration. Integrate to obtain `s_hat` and compare 70 channels: position (3), rotation-matrix entries (9, scaled by sqrt(.5)), joint angles (29), and joint velocities (29). Divide the respective squared errors by their squared tolerances `.01²,.02²,.1²,3.14²` and take the mean. There is no separate direct loss for the root linear or angular velocity and no direct `MSE(Delta,measuredDelta)`. The rotation term `.5||R_hat-R||_F²=2(1-cos(theta))` is locally approximately `theta²` and respects the equivalence of q and −q. See `gencoord.py:146–173`.

Multistep physical and contact losses use `sum(mask*loss)/sum(mask)`. Seven transitions correspond to eight upstream state frames. Training windows stay within reset boundaries. State predictions feed the next step recursively, without substituting the actual next state at each step.

The physical-state supervision can be implemented as follows.

```text
L_phys_one = mean(concat(
    (p_hat-p_true)^2 / 0.01^2,                         # 3 channels
    (sqrt(0.5)*(R_hat-R_true)).flatten()^2 / 0.02^2,   # 9 channels
    (qj_hat-qj_true)^2 / 0.1^2,                       # 29 channels
    (dqj_hat-dqj_true)^2 / 3.14^2                     # 29 channels
))
L_phys = sum(valid_mask * L_phys_one) / sum(valid_mask)
```

First average the 70 channels, then average valid times and samples. Integration indirectly constrains the consistency of position with velocity, a property lost when directly predicting a 71-dimensional successor. The 68-dimensional dynamics features omit global XY translation and yaw. The integrated global state still carries those coordinates for terrain queries, navigation, and rewards.

## 6. Differentiable visual dynamics in imagination: InstinctMJ latents

The implementation that brings images into differentiable imagination comes from the [pinned InstinctMJ Parkour SuperMimic runner](https://github.com/project-instinct/InstinctMJ/blob/03563ee02665f327425106372264070315673748/src/instinct_mj/rl/supermimic/parkour/runner.py) and `supermimic/networks.py` in its parent directory. The predicted state contains a latent for the full history of observed depth images. The decoder is used exclusively for reconstruction training. Input derivatives, parameter updates, and stop-gradient boundaries are described below.

MuJoCo and the ray caster provide data outside the actor's PyTorch BPTT graph. Imagination uses latent dynamics. It does not differentiate the physical renderer, predict RGB, or read future physical camera images.

Let `I_t` be the **joint stack** of eight frames available to the actor at time t, `E_eta` the online CNN, and `D_xi` the training-only decoder.

`z_t=E_eta(I_t)`.

`[Delta_s,c_hat,Delta_z]=F_phi(norm(physical_input), norm(z_t))`.

`s_{t+1}=GenCoordIntegrate(s_t,Delta_s)` and `z_{t+1}=z_t+Delta_z*dz_std`.

One 128-dimensional z represents the entire eight-frame stack. An imagined step predicts its successor directly, without decoding and re-encoding a frame or invoking the camera. See `src/wmac_perceptive/latent_models.py:207–212`.

Reconstruction uses `L_rec=mean(abs(D_xi(E_eta(I))-I))`. This is the only term that trains `eta` and `xi`. Up to 512 valid reconstruction stacks are used. The decoder is Linear128→(32×5×8)+ELU, ConvTranspose32→32 with k3/s2/p1/outputpad(0,1)+ELU, ConvTranspose32→16 with k3/s2/p1/outputpad(1,1)+ELU, then Conv16→8 with k3/p1. The default sigmoid output has spatial dimensions 18×32. See `instinct_latent.py:24–58`.

The world model recomputes and detaches visual targets using the **current online** encoder E.

`z0=sg(E(I0))` and `z_target[k]=sg(E(I_next[k]))`.

`L_z=(1/B)*sum_{b,k} mask[b,k]*mean_j((z_hat[b,k,j]-z_target[b,k,j])²)/max(mean_j Var_{b,k}(z_target),1e-6)`.

The denominator is a **scalar mean** of variances across latent dimensions. Do not normalize each dimension separately. The time dimension is summed and the total divided by B. Averaging over valid steps would change the multistep loss. The physical loss intentionally uses a different scale and averages over valid steps. See `instinct_latent.py:87–107` and `latent_execution.py:185–222`.

EMA statistics use `rate=.01`: `z_mean←lerp(mean(z))`, `z_std←lerp(max(std(z),1e-3))`, and `dz_std←lerp(max(sqrt(sum(mask*dz²)/sum(mask)),1e-3))`. The first two follow upstream and have no mask weighting. The dz RMS is mask-weighted. All updates run under `no_grad`. See `instinct_latent.py:61–84`.

`L_WM=L_physical+L_contact+1*L_z+1*L_rec`. The contact loss `L_contact=SmoothL1(log1p(c_hat),log1p(clamp_min(c_real,0)))` is averaged over 13 terms. The world-model optimizer owns `world_model + actor.vision + latent_decoder`. Detached targets ensure that **E receives only reconstruction gradients**. Storing old z values as replay targets would misalign supervision when the encoder's coordinates change. Replay stores preprocessed depth stacks/shared frames as uint8 by default, then converts to float and divides by 255 on sampling.

`prepare_shared` in `latent_execution.py:147–183` removes duplicate encoding. Rows selected for reconstruction retain their encoder graph. A detached view of the same tensor serves as the world-model target. Sharing the forward computation does not send the world-model loss gradient into E.

### 6.1 Where actor gradients stop in the visual pathway

`features_latent` executes `torch.cat((proprio, latent.detach()),-1)` in `src/wmac_perceptive/latent_models.py:75–82`. Four consequences follow.

- `d action_t / d z_t` is zero on this actor branch. The actor loss updates neither E, the decoder, nor the world-model parameters.
- The recurrent latent in `F_phi` remains attached. `d z_{t+1}/d a_t` exists, and the next `F_s(s_{t+1},a_{t+1},z_{t+1})` still reads that attached z.
- This preserves the input-derivative path `a_t→F_z→z_{t+1}→F_s(later physical state)→reward/value`. Stop-gradient cuts the branch `a_t→F_z→z_{t+1}→Actor_{t+1}` at the actor's visual input.
- Differentiable forward kinematics (FK) updates proprioception from the predicted physical state, preserving `a_t→s_{t+1}→proprio_{t+1}→Actor_{t+1}`.

This differentiable latent world model has an explicit visual stop-gradient, so claims of uninterrupted end-to-end gradients through future images would be incorrect. `tests/test_perceptive_latent_models.py:217` verifies that the world-model latent retains derivatives with respect to actions and inputs, and that these derivatives disappear on the actor's visual-input branch.

### 6.2 Implementation of visual latents and training targets

The following excerpts from `src/wmac_perceptive/latent_models.py` illustrate three distinct gradient boundaries that the reproduction must preserve.

```python
# Actor visual input: stop-gradient is intentional.
def features_latent(self, proprio_history, latent):
    return torch.cat((proprio_history.to(latent.dtype), latent.detach()), -1)

# The world model reads an attached latent.
def inputs_latent(self, state, action, context, latent):
    raw = self._physical_inputs(state, action, context)
    if self.reference_inputs:  # Current v3
        dim = self.in_norm.mean.numel()  # 97
        physical = torch.cat((self.in_norm(raw[..., :dim]), raw[..., dim:]), -1)
    else:  # Historical v1/v2
        physical = self.in_norm(raw)
    return torch.cat((physical,
                      (latent.to(state.dtype)-self.z_mean)/self.z_std), -1)

# The next world-model step reads next_latent with input derivatives intact.
def step_with_latent(self, state, action, context, latent):
    prediction = run_mlp(self.net,
        self.inputs_latent(state, action, context, latent), self.precision)
    next_state = self.integrate(state, prediction[..., :35])
    contact = F.softplus(prediction[..., 35:35+self.num_contact])
    next_latent = latent + prediction[..., 35+self.num_contact:] * self.dz_std
    return next_state, contact, next_latent
```

The exact latent loss reduction is implemented in `src/wmac_perceptive/instinct_latent.py:87` and `latent_execution.py:185`. The caller generates `target` using the current E under `no_grad`.

```python
# [B,K,128]. Compute a variance per latent dimension, then take their scalar mean.
flat = target.flatten(0, 1)
scale = flat.var(0, correction=1 if flat.shape[0] > 1 else 0).mean()
scale = scale.clamp(min=1e-6)
latent_errors = (predicted-target).square().mean(-1) / scale

# Sum across steps and average over B. A valid-step average changes the loss.
latent_loss = (latent_errors*mask).sum() / mask.shape[0]

# Reconstruction separately trains the online encoder and decoder.
reconstruction = (decoder(encoder(stacks))-stacks).abs().flatten(1).mean(-1)
reconstruction = masked_mean(reconstruction, reconstruction_mask)
loss = physical_loss + contact_loss + latent_loss + reconstruction
```

Image history must respect resets. Collection first captures the **pre-reset** `next_depth_frame` as the transition target, then reads the new post-reset image for done environments and fills the new history. Using a reset image for the terminal transition would corrupt the target. Frames from the previous episode must also stay out of the new episode's eight-frame stack. See `latent_training.py:50–103`.


### 6.3 Optional attention actor: state-conditioned readout and spatial/temporal information

Start a new experiment with the following command.

```bash
python scripts/train_wmac_perceptive.py \
  --execution-profile supermimic --hiking-training-version 3 \
  --actor-type transformer --run-name hiking_v3_attention
```

This option replaces only `actor.policy`. The online CNN encoder, world model's physical/latent predictions, and stop-gradient rules stay the same. The policy head has 167,069 parameters, excluding the CNN encoder. See `src/wmac_perceptive/attention_policy.py`.

#### 6.3.1 Token construction

Convert the 768-dimensional term-major history to eight chronological frames with `unpack_hiking_proprio_history`. A direct `reshape(8,96)` would mix terms and times. Each 96-dimensional frame contains angular velocity (3), gravity (3), command (3), joint position (29), joint velocity (29), and previous action (29).

```text
P_i = Linear_96_to_128(proprio_history[i])    i=0..7
V = Linear_128_to_128(stop_gradient(z))
C = Linear_3_to_128(latest_proprio[6:9])
R = P_7 + C

T = concat_tokens(P_0,...,P_7,V,C,R) + learned_position[11,128]
```

There are eleven 128-dimensional tokens: eight proprioceptive history tokens, one joint depth latent, one current command, and one readout token. The readout depends on the latest state and command, so it differs from a constant CLS token. Each proprioceptive frame already includes a command. The extra C token provides a second, explicit conditioning path. Both inputs are intentional.

Temporal fusion covers eight proprioceptive frames (7×20 ms = 140 ms) and a joint eight-frame vision history (stride 5, span 700 ms). The CNN first compresses spatial image information into a single z128. Attention receives neither an 18×32 grid of spatial patch tokens nor one visual token per frame. The Transformer is a policy head over these features. The world model retains its own architecture.

#### 6.3.2 Computation in a single attention block

The configuration uses one pre-norm block, 4 heads of dimension 32, a 256-unit FFN, GELU, zero dropout, and no causal mask. Every token represents history available at the current instant, so unmasked attention has no access to future images.

```text
N = LayerNorm(T)
Q = Linear_Q(N_readout)                 # Only the readout query, shape [4,1,32]
K,V = Linear_KV(N_all_tokens)           # Keys and values for all 11 tokens
A = softmax(Q*K^T / sqrt(32))           # Normalize each head over the 11 tokens
U = R_with_position + Linear_O(A*V)     # residual
H = U + Linear_256_to_128(GELU(Linear_128_to_256(LayerNorm(U))))
a_raw = Linear_128_to_29(H)
```

The final action layer initializes its default weights scaled by .05 and its bias to zero to reduce early joint deviation. No output tanh is used.

Computing only the final query is an execution optimization. In a full 11×11 self-attention matrix, the action head reads only the last token. With a **single block and token-wise FFN/LayerNorm**, other query outputs have no downstream consumer or second layer through which to influence the readout. Keeping all 11 keys/values and omitting the other 10 queries therefore preserves the readout and its derivatives with respect to all inputs and parameters. A second attention block would invalidate this equivalence if other token outputs were still omitted.

The implementation is shown below.

```python
# attention_policy.py:83–98
normalized = self.attention_norm(tokens)
query = self.query(normalized[:, -1:]).reshape(
    -1, 1, self.NUM_HEADS, self.head_dim).transpose(1, 2)
key, value = self.key_value(normalized).reshape(
    -1, self.NUM_TOKENS, 2, self.NUM_HEADS, self.head_dim,
).permute(2, 0, 3, 1, 4).unbind(0)
logits = (query @ key.transpose(-1, -2)) * self.attention_scale
weights = torch.softmax(logits, dim=-1).to(value.dtype)
attended = (weights @ value).reshape(-1, 1, self.EMBED_DIM)
fused = readout + self.attention_output(attended)
fused = fused + self.feedforward(self.feedforward_norm(fused))
action = self.output(fused)
```

#### 6.3.3 The visual stop-gradient in the attention actor

`LatentPerceptiveActor.features_latent` executes `concat(proprio,z.detach())` before calling the attention head. The actor stops gradients at the same point for actual images and imagined latents. Its visual projection still receives policy-parameter gradients, which cannot propagate into the input z or the image encoder.

```text
Active:  loss_actor -> attention_visual_projection_weight
Stopped: loss_actor -> attention_visual_input -> z -> encoder
Active:  loss_actor -> attention_history/KV/Q -> predicted_proprio -> physical_WM
Active:  a_t -> predicted_z_(t+1) -> later_physical_WM -> reward/value
Stopped: a_t -> predicted_z_(t+1) -> later_Actor_visual_input
```

When called by itself, `PerceptiveAttentionPolicy` can have a nonzero latent-input derivative. In the full actor, the upstream `detach` sets that derivative to zero. A successful attention unit test for the latent-input gradient does not justify removing stop-gradient from the integrated actor.

Deployment requires the image encoder and attention policy head. The training decoder, world model, discriminator, and critic do not produce deployed actions. The ONNX raw-ring interface supports attention, preserves the existing depth preprocessing and term-major history inputs, and runs without a world model in the deployment process.

## 7. AMP, the discriminator, and direct style gradients

A Hiking frame `f(s)` has 67 features ordered as `[gravity_body3, q_j-default29, .05*(v_j-default_v)29, torso_v_body3, torso_omega_body3]`. Ten frames spaced by 20 ms span 180 ms. See `hiking_amp.py:14–46`.

Flatten in **term-major** order: first the 10×3 gravity values, then the 10×29 joint positions, and so on. A direct `(10,67).flatten()` is frame-major. Both vectors have 670 dimensions but different semantics. Policy linear velocity uses the torso center of mass. Expert velocity is computed by differencing torso-origin poses. This source difference is intentional. AMP uses no running normalization and adds no terrain-height or contact features. See `state.py:90–100`.

### 7.1 From motion distributions to the least-squares discriminator

AMP fits the distribution of short policy motion windows to that of demonstration windows without requiring a match to a specific reference frame at each instant. Let p_E(w) and p_pi(w) denote the demonstration and policy window densities. With sufficient discriminator capacity and no regularization, the least-squares optimum can be found pointwise.

```text
L_D = 1/2 integral [p_pi(w) (D(w)+1)^2
                   + p_E(w) (D(w)-1)^2] dw

d L_D / d D(w) = p_pi(w) (D(w)+1) + p_E(w) (D(w)-1)

Setting the derivative to zero gives
D*(w) = [p_E(w)-p_pi(w)] / [p_E(w)+p_pi(w)]
```

Where a window occurs only in demonstrations, D* approaches +1. Where it is produced only by the current policy, D* approaches −1. Equal densities give D*=0. These scores express distributional imitation, rather than a per-frame tracking error. The implemented discriminator has finite capacity, gradient penalties (GP), and parameter regularization. Its actual score can lie outside [−1,1].

The framework maps the score to a bounded, nonnegative reward. It retains AMP's distribution-matching motivation and updates the actor using pathwise derivatives through a differentiable world model. The original AMP paper instead uses a model-free PPO policy update. The ten-frame style window is specific to the Hiking implementation.

Let w be the complete history. The discriminator is `D_psi:670→1024 ReLU→512 ReLU→1`, with expert target +1 and policy target −1.

`L_LS=.5*( E_policy[(D(w)+1)²]+E_expert[(D(w)-1)²] )`.

`L_GP=5*E_{w in concat(policy,expert)}[||grad_w D(w)||²]`.

The GP penalizes the squared gradient norm at the concatenated policy and expert samples. It uses neither WGAN-GP's `(||grad||-1)²` nor interpolated samples nor an expert-only penalty. `autograd.grad(score.sum(),examples,create_graph=True)` builds a graph that supports a further derivative with respect to D's parameters. See `amp_execution.py:14–19`.

`L_reg=3e-4*sum_{all D parameters}||p||² + .04*||W_head||²`. The first term covers the head and biases, so the head receives the extra term as well. Both are explicit L2 losses. In `runner.py:187–190`, the base optimizer is overridden with a single parameter group: `AdamW(lr=1e-4, betas=(.9,.999), weight_decay=.01)`. Keep both the explicit L2 terms and AdamW's decoupled weight decay.

The style reward is `r_amp=.25*max(0, 1-.25*(D(w)-1)²)`. The default outer weights are `task_weight=style_weight=1`.

Substituting the ideal D* gives the direction of distribution matching.

```text
D*(w)-1 = -2*p_pi(w)/(p_E(w)+p_pi(w))

r_amp(D*) = 0.25 * [1 - (p_pi(w)/(p_E(w)+p_pi(w)))^2]

When p_pi = p_E, D*=0 and r_amp=0.1875.
When p_pi greatly exceeds p_E, D* approaches -1 and the reward approaches 0.
```

A discriminator mean near zero can therefore indicate balanced distributions. Proximity to +1 alone is insufficient to assess imitation. The expression describes the ideal unregularized discriminator pointwise. A finite network in nonstationary training need not attain those values.

In the unclipped interval `-1<D<3`, `dr_amp/dD=-(.25/2)*(D-1)`. Outside it the derivative is zero. At D=−1 and 3, PyTorch returns boundary subgradients +0.25 and −0.25 respectively. Premature saturation can nearly eliminate the direct style gradient. `style_zero_gradient_fraction` counts `D<=-1 or D>=3` as a diagnostic, including the boundaries where the clamp subgradient is nonzero. The reward is bounded in `[0,.25]` and has a separate definition from discriminator loss.

The actor update requires the following derivative.

`d r_amp/dtheta=(dr_amp/dD)*(dD/df)*(df/ds)*(ds/da)*(da/dtheta)`.

Stacked history means that a future state influences the scores of multiple subsequent windows. D's parameters psi are fixed during this update, and `dL_actor/dpsi` is not stored. **Preserve dD/dinput.** Set the D parameters to `requires_grad=False` while keeping autograd enabled for D's forward pass. The style reward, FK outputs, and intermediate AMP features must remain attached. The default is `direct_style_grad=True`. Only the `no_direct_style_grad` ablation explicitly detaches style, while retaining its forward value and its contribution to critic targets. See `PerceptiveRunner.imagine/update_actor_critic` and `networks.py:102–116`.

During discriminator training, policy and expert histories serve as labeled data. `concat(...).detach().requires_grad_(True)` builds a fresh leaf whose input gradient supplies GP, isolating the policy and world model from D's training loss. The discriminator and actor updates need different gradient boundaries. PPO's no-grad reward implementation is unsuitable as a direct replacement.

### 7.2 Hiking AMP update budget, observations, and demonstration sampling in v3

The LSGAN, GP, L2, AdamW, and style-reward formulas match the November 17 embedded implementation. The input is 10×67 in term-major order. D has ReLU hidden layers of 1,024 and 512 units. Explicit L2 coefficients are 3e-4 on all parameters and .04 on head weights. A single AdamW parameter group uses lr=1e-4, betas=(.9,.999), and weight_decay=.01. GP has coefficient 5 and uses a fresh leaf from concat(policy,expert), with `create_graph` for second derivatives. D has no gradient clipping.

The actor phase still freezes D's parameters and preserves `dD/dinput`. AMP style contributes directly to BPTT. The optional attention head leaves this direction intact and does not propagate the discriminator training loss into the actor.

V3 changes which real samples D receives. Its post-step observations from `env.step` include interval events and reset. At termination/reset, D uses the new initial motion window, with all ten frames filled from the reset observation. Real world-model supervision still uses the terminal transition before reset.

```text
Physical action -> actual pre-reset successor -> WM next_state/next_depth target
                -> events and reset -> post-step observation -> v3 discriminator policy window
```

`HikingAmpFeatureCache(post_step_observations=True)` obtains the post-step value from the next collection state. At the current replay head, the last row reads `adapter.state` directly. A reset row refills the entire history. Keep these post-step samples separate from the world model's pre-reset `next_state` and depth transition targets.

With the default `walking_expert_source=pre_hiking_local_walk_turn_v2`, the shared expert pool combines the full Hiking motion and the historical local walking/turning motions, including both originals and mirrors. It samples uniformly over valid contiguous ten-frame windows, each confined to one clip. `standing_source=none` omits the old static standing CSV. A valid expert window is paired once with each real sample and reused over five epochs.

Starting a new experiment with `--walking-expert-source none` selects only the official reference, with one episode cursor per environment. A reset picks a continuous start time uniformly from the first 90% of the trajectory duration and chooses a mirror by Bernoulli sampling. The cursor advances at 50 Hz and rounds to a frame index. A robot reset fills ten frames with the same initial state. Running out of reference frames restarts only the reference timeline. Record this distribution separately from the default pool even though both include the official NPZ.

Each budget block contains 24 fresh vector steps and uses 5 epochs × 4 logical minibatches. At N=4096, a logical minibatch contains 24,576 policy samples and their expert counterparts. Each block gives 20 discriminator optimizer updates. The execution microbatch size is 512. Weight each microbatch's loss by its sample fraction within the logical minibatch, accumulate gradients, add explicit L2 once, and take one optimizer step. The 24,576/512=48 execution microbatches still form a single update. V3 checks the cursor after every physical step, independently of learner events, and leaves a final block shorter than 24 steps pending. Since 1,000,000 % 24 = 16, a fresh run can finish with 16 pending vector steps under normal operation. The older v2 protocol flushes the short final block.

### 7.3 Second-order discriminator gradients and first-order actor input gradients

The discriminator core is in `src/wmac_perceptive/amp_execution.py:14`. Detaching the data into a fresh leaf makes input gradients available for GP while keeping the discriminator loss out of the policy and world model.

```python
examples = torch.cat((policy, expert), 0).detach().requires_grad_(True)
score = discriminator(examples).squeeze(-1)
prediction = .5*((score[:count]+1).square().mean()
                +(score[count:]-1).square().mean())
grad = torch.autograd.grad(score.sum(), examples, create_graph=True)[0]
penalty = 5.0*grad.square().sum(-1).mean()

# Accumulate prediction loss and GP by each microbatch's fraction of the logical batch.
((prediction+penalty)*(count/logical_count)).backward()
# After all microbatches, add parameter regularization once and call AdamW.step() once.
```

Actor training uses D's gradients differently. In `src/wmac_perceptive/runner.py:928–939` the following runs with D's parameters frozen and autograd enabled.

```python
# amp_next depends on the differentiable predicted state. Appending it preserves the graph.
amp_history = torch.cat((amp_history[:, 1:], amp_next[:, None]), 1)
window = flatten_history(amp_history)
score = discriminator(window).squeeze(-1)
style = 0.25*(1-0.25*(score-1).square()).clamp_min(0)
reward = task + style       # Current default: direct_style_grad=True
```

The clipped reward and its derivatives are

```text
r_amp(D) = 0.25 * max(0, 1 - 0.25*(D-1)^2)

D in (-1, 3): dr_amp/dD = -0.125*(D-1)
D < -1 or D > 3: dr_amp/dD = 0
D = 1: r_amp = 0.25, dr_amp/dD = 0
D = -1 or D = 3: r_amp = 0, with PyTorch boundary derivatives +0.25 and -0.25, respectively
```

The internal style-reward coefficient is `.25`. The outer `style_weight` is 1. The task reward is multiplied by the `.02` control period once. AMP receives no additional time-step multiplier. Changing either convention significantly changes the relative gradient scale.

### 7.4 Gradient differences from the original PPO-AMP

Model-free AMP/PPO collects simulated trajectories and scalar rewards, then computes advantages. Its policy gradient uses log probabilities and generally takes no state derivative of the reward generator.

```text
policy-gradient estimate = E[grad_theta log pi_theta(a|o) * advantage]
PPO ratio = pi_theta(a|o) / pi_old(a|o)
PPO surrogate = E[min(ratio*A, clip(ratio,1-epsilon,1+epsilon)*A)]
```

Here the policy update directly computes `grad_theta J(F_phi, D_psi, V_omega, pi_theta)`. Computing rewards under `no_grad` is appropriate in the older PPO implementation. Reusing it here would remove the required `dD/dstate`. The discriminator itself still trains on real data, with no D-loss gradient flowing through the imagined model into the actor. Official SuperMimic's motion-tracking reward admits analytic derivatives. This framework replaces part of the scoring function with AMP's frozen-parameter discriminator, preserves its input derivatives, and adds a visual latent state. These changes affect the learning method as well as the network architecture.

## 8. SuperMimic imagined actor–critic: returns, BPTT, and targets

Sample initial `s0,context0,proprio_history,I0,command modes,AMP history` from real replay. Initialize `z0=sg(E(I0))`. The fixed horizon is H=32. The historical adaptive horizon and model-loss gate are inactive.

Let `d_t` be the soft termination probability, `c_t=1-d_t`, and `S_0=1, S_{t+1}=S_t*c_t`. Weight the reward with survival `S_t` from before this step. This still counts the immediate reward on a step that terminates the episode.

`J(theta)= E[sum_{t=0}^{H-1} gamma^t S_t (r_task,t+r_amp,t) + gamma^H S_H min(V_omega(x_H),V_max)]`.

`L_actor=-mean(J)`. Optional MoE router regularization is evaluated only at real starting states, and all its coefficients currently equal zero.

Write the augmented recurrent state as `y=(s,context,history,z)`. Its first-order backward dependencies satisfy

`dy_next/dtheta = F_y*dy/dtheta + F_a*(pi_theta + pi_proprio*dproprio/dtheta)`.

Stop-gradient on the actor's latent branch removes the extra `pi_z*dz/dtheta` term. The latent-to-physics Jacobian in F_y remains intact.

`dJ/dtheta` receives contributions through immediate task reward, AMP, survival, and the terminal critic input. `dS_next=c*dS + S*dc`. Detaching cumulative survival removes the gradient that attributes a longer future return to safer actions. Detaching the final critic observation would make bootstrapping a value with no gradient to guide the actor. Detach the intermediate observation copies saved for critic training, and retain the live terminal observation. See `src/wmac_perceptive/runner.py:886–956` and `reference_policy_step.py:24–49`. Each step evaluates the reward on the successor of the current command/action before updating the next command and critic observation.

The actor update uses `frozen_parameters(world_model,D,critic)`. Freezing module parameters preserves the input Jacobians. A code assertion checks that all their `.grad` values are `None` after the actor update. `opt_actor` owns only `actor.policy`. `opt_model` owns the world model, visual encoder, and decoder. See `src/wmac_perceptive/runner.py:148–161,1307–1415`.

The critic computes generalized advantage estimation (GAE) targets under `no_grad`: `delta_t=r_t+gamma*c_t V_old(x_next)-V_old(x_t)`, `A_t=delta_t+gamma*lambda*c_t*A_next`, and `target_t=min(A_t+V_old(x_t),V_max)`. Lambda is .95 and gamma .99. Clip only the upper bound and retain negative values. Train with MSE over 5 epochs × 4 minibatches. The default `real_critic_coef=0` uses imagined targets exclusively. See `reference_training.py:98–117`, `src/wmac_perceptive/runner.py:949–956`, and `src/wmac_perceptive/macro_execution.py:305–329`.

The H32 return, survival recursion, GAE, gradient through the terminal critic input, and optimizer ownership of actor, world model, encoder, and discriminator are unchanged. The critic feature width and v3 clipping value are updated.

```text
positive_weights = 2 + 2 + 3 + 0.5 + 0.4 = 7.9
V_clip = (task_weight * dt * positive_weights
          + style_weight * amp_reward_coef) / (1-gamma)
       = (0.02*7.9 + 0.25)/0.01
       = 40.8
```

V3 follows the official code's sum-of-positive-weights construction for a reference clipping threshold. It gives no strict mathematical upper bound on all unclipped local Hiking rewards. The raw `feet_air_time` term can exceed 1, and a negative weight on `stand_still` can combine with a negative offset to give a positive contribution. V2 added conservative corrections for these terms to obtain 61.4. That earlier strict-bound argument does not apply to 40.8.

Bootstrap uses `clamp(max=V_clip)`. GAE labels receive the upper cap after recursion. Negative values remain intact. PyTorch gives the value branch derivative zero strictly above the cap and one exactly at the cap. The survival branch still differentiates through multiplication by the clipped value.

### 8.1 Gradient ownership by training stage

| Update | Network parameters updated | Input derivatives retained | Stop-gradient boundaries |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| WM physical/contact/latent supervision | `world_model` | Derivatives of F with respect to its recurrent state, z, and inputs | E outputs for starting states and supervised targets |
| Image reconstruction | `actor.vision`, `latent_decoder` | All derivatives of E and decoder | Original image target is data |
| AMP discriminator | `discriminator` | D input gradient at new leaf for GP | Detach policy/expert histories |
| Imagined actor update | `actor.policy` | Input derivatives of WM, FK, D, and critic | Actor reads a detached z. Save detached critic training observations and targets. |
| Critic regression | `critic` | Critic parameter gradients only | Detach all imagined observations and GAE targets |

`src/wmac/networks.py:102` freezes parameters by temporarily setting `requires_grad=False` and restoring the original flags afterward.

```python
with frozen_parameters(world_model, discriminator, critic):
    rollout = runner.imagine(batch)
    loss_actor = -rollout["objective"].mean()
    loss_actor.backward()
    # The optimizer owns only actor.policy. opt_model trains vision.
    opt_actor.step()
```

Keep autograd enabled for `imagine` and the D and critic forward passes. Wrapping them in `torch.no_grad()` removes the world-model input derivatives, direct AMP style gradient, and terminal critic guidance. Keep WM, D, and critic parameters outside the actor optimizer to prevent the policy from increasing imagined rewards by changing the model or scorer.

### 8.2 Implementation of step returns and critic gradient boundaries

The following operations come from `src/wmac_perceptive/runner.py:886–956`. Each observation saved for critic training is detached. The final live `critic_obs` retains its graph.

```python
objective = state.new_zeros(len(state))
survival = torch.ones_like(objective)
critic_rollout = []
for step in range(horizon):
    critic_rollout.append(critic_obs.detach())
    (state, context, history, latent, action, command, contact, terminated,
     task, amp_next, critic_obs) = self._reference_step_fn(
        state, context, history, latent, batch["navigation_target"],
        batch["desired_speed"], noises[step], standing,
        random_yaw_rate=batch["random_yaw_rate"],
        random_velocity_mask=batch["random_velocity_mask"],
        previous_action=previous)
    # Compute style as shown in section 7.3.
    reward = self.cfg.task_weight*task + self.cfg.style_weight*style
    objective = objective + self.cfg.gamma**step * survival * reward
    continuation = 1 - terminated
    survival = survival * continuation
    previous = action

bootstrap = self._value(critic_obs).clamp(max=self._critic_value_ceiling)
objective = objective + self.cfg.gamma**horizon * survival * bootstrap
# Generate the critic's regression targets separately under no_grad. Its update uses a separate graph.
```

This excerpt assumes all three current gradient switches are enabled. See the original function for the complete loop and initial variables.

The soft-continuation gradient can be checked by hand.

```text
S_0 = 1
S_(t+1) = S_t * c_t

dS_(t+1)/dtheta = c_t*dS_t/dtheta + S_t*dc_t/dtheta

dJ/dtheta = sum_t gamma^t [S_t*dr_t/dtheta + r_t*dS_t/dtheta]
           + gamma^H [S_H*dV_H/dtheta + V_H*dS_H/dtheta]
```

For the actor update, critic parameters are fixed, while `dV_H/dx_H` can be nonzero. Strictly above the cap, the local derivative of the bootstrap value branch becomes zero. At exact equality, PyTorch clamp returns a derivative of one. The survival branch can still pass gradients through the clipped bootstrap value. The reference tests cover this case.


### 8.3 Piecewise differentiability and hard gates

Some reward terms and parts of the world model are only piecewise differentiable. Contact reward conditions such as `force>1`, moving/standing command branches, speed comparisons in `dont_wait`, and some terrain or clipping boundaries still use hard boolean conditions. There is no continuous derivative with respect to these gates themselves. Gradients can pass through the velocities, positions, joint states, and predicted auxiliary values within an active branch. Autograd cannot shift a threshold by differentiating through a comparison. The v2 fix specifically aligned the forward and backward behavior of the imagined **termination probability** and survival recursion. Hiking's 26 rewards retain their individual definitions.

## 9. Gradient and training protocol fixes

### 9.1 Soft termination in v3 and compatibility with earlier versions

The physical environment retains three hard failure thresholds for the torso: low height, tilt above 1 rad, and contact force above 1 N. Imagined rollouts use the same smooth probability in the forward and backward passes. Version 3 normalizes the three physical criteria, selects the most severe one, and applies a single sigmoid.

```text
h = torso_Z - min(environment_origin_Z, 0)
g_z = (R_torso^-1 * [0,0,-1])_z
F = predicted_torso_contact_force_max

u_height = 1 + (0.5-h)/0.5
u_tilt = (1+g_z)/(1-cos(1.0))
u_force = F / 1.0
u = max(u_height, u_tilt, u_force)
d = sigmoid((u-1)/0.05)
continuation = 1-d
```

At any individual physical threshold, u = 1 and the soft probability of termination is 0.5. If several criteria reach their thresholds simultaneously, the probability is still 0.5. The probabilistic OR in v2 gives a higher probability in this case. The maximum is piecewise differentiable. Usually, only the most severe criterion contributes to the gate derivative. At ties, PyTorch's `maximum` distributes the subgradient. The individual hazards therefore need not all receive gradients at a given point.

The v2 branch retains the soft OR of three sigmoids. Version 1 retains the straight-through estimator with a hard forward pass and a soft backward pass. Each version stores its own training protocol. An ordinary resume must preserve the version recorded with the weights.

### 9.2 Optimizers and attention parameter groups

The Muon/Adam implementation is identical to the November 17 version. Within each `nn.Sequential`, remove the first and last layers from its list of linear layers. Assign only the remaining `Linear.weight` tensors to Muon and all other parameters to Adam. This gives the world model (WM), critic and default MoE their respective mixed parameter groups.

The attention head's projection, Q, KV and readout are standalone linear layers. The feed-forward network contains only two linear layers, so it has no intermediate layer. Building the optimizer yields one Adam group with 23 parameter tensors and 167,069 parameters. The attention policy's Muon group is empty. The CNN and latent decoder still belong to `opt_model`, and the entire attention head belongs to `opt_actor`.

The actor uses a learning rate of 2e-4 and Adam betas (0.9, 0.95). The WM and critic default to Adam betas (0.9, 0.999). All three use constant learning rates of 2e-4. Their gradients first undergo norm clipping at 1. The actor also clips individual gradient values to ±0.1. The discriminator (D) does not clip gradients. Attention requires the MoE load-balancing and router-z regularization coefficients to be zero.

### 9.3 The v3 physical clock, replay and update counts

`--iterations` specifies the final number of vector control steps. Each vector step advances N parallel physical environments by one control step. With the defaults of 1,000,000 steps and N = 4,096, this gives up to 4,096,000,000 individual environment transitions. Each step represents 0.02 s of simulated time. Wall-clock training time depends on the machine.

`reference_loop.learn_reference` calls `collect(1)` and advances a separate AMP cursor on every step. The Ratio scheduler determines how many learner updates follow that step. At the default `utd=.4`, the first scheduled event occurs immediately and is skipped because replay contains fewer than eight frames. The Ratio clock advances without making up skipped events later. Once eight complete frames are available, learner updates occur on steps 9, 11, 14, 16, 19, and so on. Each comprises ten WM subupdates, one actor update and 20 critic minibatch updates. CLI overrides for N/B/U/K automatically recalculate UTD to maintain the default replay ratio of 16 unless `--utd` is explicitly set.

The `warmup_steps=8` field remains. The ordinary sampling loop now collects the required frames without an extra eight-step collection before learning. `iteration` and N in `model_N.pt` still count learner updates. The CSV reports sampling progress separately in `vector_step`. `sim_steps` counts individual environment transitions. Saving occurs when the learner count crosses a multiple of 1,000, with additional snapshots at the first and last vector steps. Resume continues the vector clock from the saved `sim_steps/N`.

In v3, `sample_reference_model_windows` samples eight complete observed physical states to supervise seven transitions. It first samples uniformly among environments with valid complete windows, then uniformly among valid starting points in that environment. Windows crossing a terminal, timeout, invalid transition or physical restart are rejected. A command update alone does not reset the physics. Arbitrary starting points and truncated, masked windows describe the old v2 distribution. The v3 default `validation_env_fraction=0` leaves no held-out data. It provides no estimate of zero model error. Enable and record a separate validation experiment to assess generalization.

### 9.4 Conditions for mathematical equivalence of execution optimizations

| Change | Execution optimization only? | Conditions for equivalence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Share successor FK and the next command within a step | Yes | Share local tensors for the same step without detaching or caching across steps or optimizer updates. Reward, observation, AMP and termination read the same successor. |
| Reuse four gathered critic minibatches for five epochs | Yes | Detached observations and targets stay fixed. The original schedule uses the same permutation in each epoch. Update order is preserved. |
| Stage WM inputs directly into the graph using `torch.stack(...,out=persistent_inputs)` | Yes | Raw replay labels require no gradients. Ordering, shape, dtype and schema match. Validate all schemas before writing. |
| Capture ten WM subupdates in one CUDA Graph | Yes | Re-encode with the current online E on every subupdate. A stale target z cannot be reused across all ten. Optimizer state and gradient buffer storage stay fixed. |
| Compute only the readout query in attention | Yes, for the same single attention block | Only the last token is read. All other K/V entries remain available. There is no second block or cross-token postprocessing. |
| Replace attention with MoE | No | The policy function, initialization and parameter partition change. Treat this as a separate experiment. |
| v2 to v3 robot, WM input, soft gate, value clipping, sample distribution and clock | No | Each of these changes the protocol or the mathematical operation. |

The shared FK implementation in `compiled_imagination.py:34–67` and `reference_policy_step.py:24–49` reduces six FK calls per step to two: one for the current state's command and one for the successor. Successor FK remains in the same autograd graph. The adapter does not hold graph tensors across updates. Tests compare all outputs and derivatives with respect to state, context, history, latent, previous action and actor parameters.

In `macro_execution.py:305–330`, the critic generates a permutation once, partitions the fixed features and targets into four batches, and processes them in the original order for five epochs. It still executes 20 `optimizer.step` calls. Critic weights continue to update. Each later epoch recomputes its forward pass and loss with the updated critic.

Direct WM staging in `macro_execution.py:158–194` checks each field's shape, dtype, device and `requires_grad` before writing persistent buffers. The ten prepare/loss/backward/clip/step sequences in `wm_macro_execution.py:48–70` still execute in order. The previous reconstruction loss updates E, so the next subupdate must recompute its target. Capture adds no training update. The three warmup passes count as three actual learner macro-updates.

## 10. Rewards and their imagined counterparts

### 10.1 Computation order, notation and all 26 terms

The physics timestep is 0.005 s and decimation is 4, giving a control dt of 0.02 s (50 Hz). See `src/tasks/amp_loco/amp_env_cfg.py:430-437`. The environment inherits mjlab's `ManagerBasedRlEnvCfg.scale_rewards_by_dt=True`, so its physical task reward is `r_task=0.02*Σ_i w_i*f_i`. The imagined path reads the same setting in `src/wmac/state.py:198`. `PerceptiveStateAdapter.task_reward` ultimately calls `hiking_weighted_reward` and also multiplies by 0.02 exactly once.

The current AMP style reward is `r_amp=0.25*max(0,1-(D(h)-1)^2/4)`, where h is the 670-dimensional ten-frame history. With `task_weight=style_weight=1`, the actor optimizes the per-step sum `r=r_task+r_amp` (`config.py:282-285` and `PerceptiveRunner.imagine`). **AMP receives no further dt multiplier.** The terms are added on their native scales, without a 0.25/0.75 task/style weighting or normalization to a common scale. When D is below -1 or above 3, `r_amp` and its gradient in the clipped region are zero. The total task reward has no positive-only clamp or global penalty clipping. With `action_limit=None` in v3, neither policy output nor raw exploratory action is clipped. Position targets use the actual scale and offset, and applied PD torque is clamped at the rated effort.

All 26 formulas are shared by physical simulation and imagined rollouts. The physical path uses observed successor states, applied torques, forces and timers. Imagination uses GenCoord successors and 13 supervised WM auxiliary predictions. Labels such as physical `qacc` and saturated torque must retain their original meanings. Control-step velocity differences and ideal PD estimates are unsuitable substitutes.

The authoritative definitions are in `src/tasks/amp_perceptive/hiking_rewards.py:21-34,82-144`. The physical inputs are assembled in `src/wmac_perceptive/hiking_rewards.py:44-82`. Each f below is the raw term before weighting or dt scaling. The command c = (cx, cy, cz) contains planar linear and yaw angular velocity. v is the **torso COM** linear velocity in the torso frame, and ω is torso angular velocity in that same frame. q and dq are the 29 joint positions and velocities, δq = q - q_default, and a and a_prev are the current and previous 29-dimensional actions. gT, gP and gF are unit gravity vectors in the torso, pelvis and foot frames. C_i = 1 when the maximum net force norm in the last three physics substeps exceeds 1 N. M = 1 when norm(c_xy) > 0.15 or abs(cz) > 0.15. S = 1 when norm(c_xy) < 0.15 and abs(cz) < 0.15. If both speed measures are at most 0.15 and at least one equals 0.15, both M and S are false.

| Name | w | Raw term f or definition |
|---|---:|---|
| track_lin_vel_xy_exp | 2 | exp(-norm(c_xy-v_xy)^2/0.25). The standard deviation parameter is 0.5 and the denominator is its square. |
| track_ang_vel_z_exp | 2 | exp(-(cz-ωz)²/0.25) |
| heading_error | -1 | abs(cz). Despite its source name, the term penalizes commanded yaw rate. Heading error influences it indirectly through the controller. |
| dont_wait | -0.5 | 1[cx>0.3]*(1[vx<0.15]+1[vx<0]+1[vx<-0.15]), giving 0, 1, 2 or 3. |
| is_alive | 3 | 1-terminated. Physical termination is a hard failure indicator. Imagined v3 termination is a continuous probability. |
